result:
Solution 2 is the only one that reaches the correct answer, 171; Solutions 1 and 3 give 186 and 185, which are too large.

**Condition for distinguishing two primes.** Ana can tell p from q exactly when no response is consistent with both a nonconstant p-periodic function and a nonconstant q-periodic function.

- If the equivalence relations "same residue mod p" and "same residue mod q" on the queried points have a join with at least 2 classes, a nonconstant response that is constant on each class fits both periods. Ana fails.
- If the join has one class, the only response consistent with both is a constant one. A constant response fits period p only if some residue mod p is unqueried, so that a nonconstant extension exists.

So for every pair (p, q), the bipartite graph on the queried residues must be connected, and all residues mod p or all residues mod q must be queried.

**Lower bound.** At most one prime can fail to have all its residues covered. Among 83, 89, 97, at least two are therefore fully covered. A connected graph on those two sets of residues needs at least p + q − 1 edges, and each query gives at most one edge. The cheapest such pair is (83, 89), giving n ≥ 83 + 89 − 1 = 171.

**Upper bound.** Take every query point to be a multiple of 97, so only one residue mod 97 is used. Pairs involving 97 are then connected as soon as all residues of the other prime are covered. By the Chinese remainder theorem the residues mod the other primes can be chosen independently. A spanning tree for (83, 89) uses exactly 171 points, and the remaining pairs need fewer edges, so 171 points plausibly suffice for all pairs at once. I did not verify this construction in full, and Solution 2's own verification of it is hand-waved. The answer 171 also matches my recollection of this problem.

**Solutions 1 and 3.** Both ignore that one prime may be left with some residues unqueried. That is what lets the largest pair (89, 97) be avoided, so their bound of 185 or 186 is too high.

VERDICT 1: REJECT
VERDICT 2: ACCEPT
VERDICT 3: REJECT
